the neural correlates of the social identity construct are partly shared with the neural correlates for the self, but that the overlap is only present for highly identified group members.
the neural correlates of the self-face and social identity partially overlap, and that this overlap is more pronounced for high identifiers than for low identifiers.
the neural basis of in-group and out-group perception is related to that of self and other perception, but only for high identifiers.

the neural basis of in-group and out-group perceptions.
the neural correlates that underlie social identification.
the relationship between self-perception and group membership and how these two concepts are represented in the brain.

the neural correlates of in- and self-face perception are similar for high identifiers.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain regions associated with self-perception and with social identity are overlapping, but only for high identifiers, suggesting that the brain regions involved in self-face perception may be involved in social identity only to the extent that the group is part of the self.
self-face perception and social identity are not two completely distinct constructs but that there is some overlap in the neural processes underlying them.
